title: 5 aspects of memory
content_html:
5 aspects of memory

The five most important aspects of memory are:

  1. Encoding – transforming sensory input into a format the memory system can use (visual, acoustic, semantic).
  2. Storage – maintaining information over time, considering capacity
  3. Retrieval – accessing stored information, which differs between sequential recall and associative recall
  4. Rehearsal – verbal or mental repetition that strengthens encoding and helps transfer information from short-term to long-term memory.
  5. Ecological Validity – the extent to which findings from memory research (often laboratory-based) apply to real-life situations, since many memory experiments use artificial tasks

These five highlight both the core processes (encoding, storage, retrieval, rehearsal) and the critical limitation (ecological validity) in how memory research is interpreted.

Aspect Definition / Key Idea Notes & Examples
Encoding The process of changing incoming information into a form the memory system can store (visual, acoustic, semantic). E.g., repeating a phone number aloud (acoustic); remembering the meaning of a word (semantic).
Storage How information is maintained over time, including capacity and duration. STM holds 5–9 items for up to 30 seconds (Miller, 1956); LTM has unlimited capacity and can last a lifetime.
Retrieval Getting information out of memory when needed. STM retrieval is sequential (step by step); LTM retrieval is associative (linked to context or cues).
Rehearsal Repetition of information to strengthen encoding and support transfer from STM to LTM. Saying items over and over helps retain them beyond short-term limits.
Ecological Validity The degree to which memory research findings apply to real-life settings. Lab tasks (e.g., recalling lists of random words) may not reflect how memory works in everyday life.

In reality, each step is fragile, fallible, and shaped by context. Encoding isn’t perfect, we don’t record everything we experience — attention, emotion, and bias filter what gets encoded. Storage isn’t permanent, memories can fade, distort, or be overwritten (plasticity and reconsolidation). Retrieval isn’t exact, we reconstruct, not replay. Recall is influenced by cues, mood, and current beliefs. So while “Encode–Store–Retrieve” is a clean summary, it risks implying a mechanical model. A more realistic three-word framing might be:

Select – Change – Reconstruct

  • Select what enters memory (attention + encoding).
  • Change as memories consolidate, fade, and reshape in storage.
  • Reconstruct when recalling, always influenced by present context.

Connecting Memory, Tao, and Wetlands

We can also explicity include the idea of plasticity:

Encoding → Storage → Consolidation → Retrieval → Plasticity → (feedback back to Encoding)

These five key processes of memory - Encoding, Storage, Consolidation, Retrieval, and Plasticity - mirror Taoist principles of stillness, simplicity, and change. Like wetland plants shifting with water and season, memories are encoded in still moments, stored with simplicity in neural traces, consolidated as patterns in cycles, retrieved as transformations, and reshaped through plasticity in continuous change. Just as wetlands embody resilience and adaptation, memory is not a static archive but a living, shifting landscape—each recall reshaping the past as nature reshapes itself.

  • Encoding: experiences are transformed into neural representations.
  • Storage: information is maintained across time (working/long‑term).
  • Consolidation: traces are stabilised (sleep, replay, synaptic changes).
  • Retrieval: reconstruction that can update the trace (reconsolidation).
  • Plasticity: adaptability of networks enabling formation, change, forgetting.
